name: Galantamine
lead: Galantamine is an alkaloid first isolated from snowdrop (Galanthus) bulbs in the Soviet Union in the 1940s and now also produced synthetically.[1] It is a prescription medicine for mild to moderate Alzheimer disease that works by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, which raises acetylcholine levels, and it also acts at nicotinic receptors.[1][2]

In nootropic and dream communities it is taken before or during sleep to make dreams more vivid and easier to remember, and as an aid to lucid dreaming.[1][10] Its link to appearance runs through sleep and cognition: people who use it describe it as part of routines aimed at better rest, sharper thinking and general self-improvement, and rest quality is one of the things that shapes how rested a person looks.

Published research has examined it mainly in Alzheimer disease, with smaller randomized trials in conditions such as cocaine use disorder, post-stroke aphasia and subarachnoid hemorrhage.[4][5][7][8][9] A 2018 pre-sleep study on lucid dreaming is widely shared in online forums.[11]

chain: Users report sharper cognition and more vivid dreams
angle.text: People use it as a nootropic and a lucid-dreaming aid, linking sleep experience and mental performance to how they feel and present day to day. It is a prescription drug, and these uses are off-label.

paras: Galantamine is approved to treat mild to moderate dementia of the Alzheimer type, and it has also been used in vascular dementia.[1][12] Outside that indication, online communities discuss it as a nootropic and as a pre-sleep aid for lucid dreaming.[1][13][14]

The US label describes it as a cholinesterase inhibitor indicated for mild to moderate dementia of the Alzheimer type.[12] Reviews find that the three marketed cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, galantamine, rivastigmine) have broadly similar efficacy and that the benefit is modest.[3][15]

Wikipedia describes galantamine as oneirogenic, noting that research suggests it can increase dream recall, dream self-awareness and vividness, which may help induce lucid dreams.[1] A 2018 pre-sleep study on lucid dreaming drew substantial discussion on Hacker News.[11] On the T Nation forum, posters in lucid-dreaming threads describe combining it with choline bitartrate or vitamin B6 and a short wake-and-return-to-bed routine.[13][14]

T Nation threads about brain-function supplements show galantamine appearing in multi-ingredient commercial nootropic blends alongside compounds such as huperzine A, piracetam and vinpocetine, with members debating whether such blends help memory and creativity.[16][17]

Galantamine is a weak, reversible inhibitor of acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine, so it raises acetylcholine levels in cholinergic pathways.[1][2] It has also been described as an allosteric potentiator of some nicotinic receptors, a dual mechanism; more recent studies question whether it acts as a positive allosteric modulator at human alpha4beta2 or alpha7 receptors.[1] Because acetylcholine is closely tied to REM sleep, the cholinergic effect is the usual explanation offered for its reported influence on dreams.[2]

Oral bioavailability is 80 to 100 percent, plasma protein binding is about 18 percent, and the terminal half-life is about 7 hours.[1] Roughly 75 percent is metabolized in the liver by CYP2D6 and CYP3A4, so drugs that inhibit those enzymes can raise exposure; paroxetine, a CYP2D6 inhibitor, increased bioavailability by about 40 percent. About 95 percent is excreted by the kidneys, a third of it unchanged.[1]

Galantamine is an alkaloid (C17H21NO3, molar mass about 287 g/mol) with a tertiary amine that is mostly protonated at neutral pH.[1] It occurs in the common, Caucasian and Voronov's snowdrops and other Amaryllidaceae such as daffodil, snowflake and red spider lily, but natural yields are low, around 0.1 percent by weight, so industrial synthesis is common.[1]

Common effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness and headache. Serious risks listed include allergic reactions, stomach bleeding, liver injury and chest pain.[1] The US label also warns of serious skin reactions, advises discontinuing at the first appearance of a rash, and says all patients should be considered at risk for effects on cardiac conduction, including slow heart rate and AV block, because of its vagotonic effects.[12] The label notes that adequate data in pregnant women are lacking, and that animal studies showed developmental effects.[12]

Galantamine was isolated from snowdrop bulbs in the Soviet Union in the 1940s.[1] Bulgarian chemist Dimitar Paskov is credited with first extracting it and proposing its medical use in 1959, the year the first industrial process was developed; full-scale synthesis was not scaled and optimized until the 1990s.[1] Two large placebo-controlled Alzheimer trials appeared in Neurology in 2000, and a derivative, benzgalantamine (Zunveyl, formerly ALPHA-1062), was approved by the FDA in July 2024.[1][4][5]

Galantamine's journey from a Bulgarian-extracted snowdrop alkaloid to a marketed Alzheimer drug included a 2004 Bulgarian trial of Nivalin, a product whose active ingredient is galantamine, and the December 2023 acceptance of an FDA application for the prodrug ALPHA-1062 before its 2024 approval as Zunveyl.[1] In dream communities, the 2018 trial marks the point at which the compound moved from forum anecdote toward published research.[27]

The best-known study of galantamine in dream practice is a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial by Stephen LaBerge, Kristen LaMarca and Benjamin Baird, published in PLOS ONE in August 2018. It enrolled 121 adults with high dream recall and an interest in lucid dreaming, recruited from workshops run by the Lucidity Institute. Over three nights each participant received an inactive placebo or one of two galantamine dose levels in counterbalanced order, taken after about four and a half hours of sleep, followed by a half-hour awake period and a mnemonic lucid-dream technique on returning to sleep.[27]

Participants reported at least one lucid dream on 14 percent of placebo nights, 27 percent at the lower dose and 42 percent at the higher dose; the authors estimated a baseline of about 4 percent from participants' prior six months of recall. Dream recall, sensory vividness and complexity were also higher on galantamine. Mild side effects such as gastrointestinal upset, insomnia and next-day fatigue were reported by 12 percent of participants on active doses and 3 percent on placebo.[27]

The authors listed limitations: the study ran outside a sleep laboratory, without polysomnography, and relied on self-reported lucidity; the participants were a motivated group from a single workshop setting; and the contributions of the induction technique and the interrupted sleep were not tested separately.[27] Baird told Discover magazine that the results were not expected to be that strong, and noted that expectation plays a strong role in lucid dreaming.[28] On Hacker News, commenters raised the same points, including the instrument being developed by the lead author and the possibility that side effects let participants guess their condition.[11]

Wikipedia's lucid dream article describes the 2018 trial as the only one of its kind and places it among induction methods such as wake-back-to-bed and mnemonic induction, with a 2022 meta-analysis identifying 14 induction techniques.[29] A 2023 systematic review by Tan and Fan is cited on galantamine's own Wikipedia page for oneirogenic effects.[1]

The wiki's interest in galantamine runs through the sleep and cognition chain: people who use it describe aims such as better recall of dreams, clearer thinking and more structured self-improvement routines, and sleep quality is one of the things that shapes how rested a person looks. Lucid-dreaming commentators in the Hacker News thread, however, report that practising lucid dreaming can itself disturb sleep, with some describing poorer sleep quality, waking in the night, exhaustion, more sleep paralysis and false awakenings, while others describe it as enjoyable.[11][29] Lucid dreaming sources add that sleep paralysis is a distinct experience reported at least once by about 7.6 percent of the general population, and that long-term effects of practising lucid dreaming have not been extensively studied.[29]

Galantamine reached appearance- and optimisation-minded forums through two routes. One was nootropic discussion, where the cholinergic mechanism made it a candidate for stacks alongside other compounds; on T Nation, threads about brain boosters mention it among blend ingredients.[16][17] The other was lucid dreaming, where the 2018 trial gave a prescription dementia drug a published dream-induction result that circulated on Hacker News and in press features.[11][28] Forum participants frequently note that it is a prescription medicine and that it has labelled warnings, including skin reactions and cardiac conduction effects.[12][13][17]

The foundation for galantamine's approval is a pair of randomised, placebo-controlled trials in Alzheimer disease published in Neurology in 2000: a 5-month study by the Galantamine USA-10 group and a 6-month study with a 6-month extension by the Galantamine USA-1 group.[4][5] A 2008 systematic review and meta-analysis of 26 studies on donepezil, galantamine and rivastigmine reported that placebo-controlled data supported modest overall benefits for stabilising or slowing decline in cognition, function, behaviour and global change, and that the few head-to-head comparisons gave conflicting results; its indirect comparison found a better relative risk of global response with donepezil and rivastigmine than with galantamine.[15] A 2021 review concluded that the three marketed cholinesterase inhibitors have similar efficacy and that the benefit is mild, and a 2024 meta-analysis of Alzheimer drugs reported that cholinesterase inhibitors improved cognitive function.[3][18] A 2015 systematic review of Lewy body dementia found beneficial effects for donepezil and rivastigmine and descriptive evidence of benefits for galantamine.[19]

Outside dementia, trials are small. The SAHRANG pilot, published in 2025, enrolled 60 patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage in a multicentre, double-masked design, assigning them within 72 hours of onset to galantamine at one of two dose levels or placebo for 90 days, with tolerability and safety as the primary outcomes.[7] Randomised trials have also examined galantamine in cocaine use disorder and in chronic post-stroke aphasia,[8][9] and a 2024 review of non-stimulant treatments for adult ADHD reported negative findings for galantamine.[6] Registered trials have looked at ADHD, bipolar disorder and cognition around electroconvulsive therapy, and a bioequivalence study compared generic and brand tablets.[20][21][22][23]

For the dream-related use, the main human work is the 2018 PLOS ONE pre-sleep lucid-dreaming crossover study of 121 adults, described above, in which the share reporting a lucid dream rose from 14 percent on placebo nights to 27 and 42 percent at the two galantamine dose levels.[27][11]

For its approved use, reviews describe galantamine as one of three cholinesterase inhibitors with broadly similar and modest effects on cognition, daily function and behaviour in mild to moderate Alzheimer disease, and the drugs are used as symptomatic treatment rather than as a way of halting the disease.[2][3][15] An extended-release capsule form is described on the US label, and the dual action on acetylcholinesterase and nicotinic receptors is the pharmacological rationale offered for its use.[1][12]

In appearance-minded communities, users describe galantamine as a tool for dream recall and mental clarity rather than a physical enhancer; where a link to looks is made, it runs through focus, sleep and habit-building rather than any direct effect on the body.[13][14][16]
Galantamine is prescription-only in the US and EU, and Brazil lists it in Class C1.[1] The main brand name is Razadyne (earlier Reminyl); benzgalantamine is sold as Zunveyl.[1]

subs.h: Use in nootropic and dream communities
paras: On T Nation, galantamine shows up in lucid-dreaming threads and in discussions of commercial nootropic blends, typically alongside choline sources or B vitamins.[13][14][16][17] Users describe the aim as stronger dream recall and awareness; participants in the same threads often note it is a prescription Alzheimer medicine and ask each other to read up on it first.[17]

Wikipedia describes galantamine as oneirogenic, and the dream-enhancement angle has been the main route by which a prescription dementia drug reached online self-experimentation communities.[1] Participants in the T Nation threads often pair it with choline sources or B vitamins and note that it is a prescription medicine; the US label warns of serious skin reactions and of effects on cardiac conduction.[12][13][14][17]

timeline.event: Galantamine isolated from snowdrop plants in the Soviet Union.[1]
Dimitar Paskov credited with extracting galantamine and proposing its medical use; first industrial process developed.[1]
Two large placebo-controlled Alzheimer trials published in Neurology.[4][5]
A trial of Nivalin, whose active ingredient is galantamine, is reported from Bulgaria.[1]
LaBerge, LaMarca and Baird publish a 121-person pre-sleep lucid-dreaming crossover study in PLOS ONE; it is discussed widely online.[27][11]
FDA accepts the new drug application for the galantamine prodrug ALPHA-1062 (December); a systematic review of galantamine and oneirogenic effects appears.[1]
Benzgalantamine (Zunveyl) approved by the FDA for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease (July).[1]
The SAHRANG pilot in aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage is published.[7]

lore.intro: On T Nation and Hacker News, galantamine is discussed as a lucid-dreaming aid and as an ingredient in nootropic stacks.[13][14][11][16]

claims.claim: Taken before sleep, galantamine makes dreams more vivid and helps trigger lucid dreams
claims.believers: Posters describe a routine of galantamine with choline bitartrate before a short return to sleep in the early morning, reporting intense, memorable dreams.[14] Others pair it with vitamin B6 and meditation.[13]
claims.experts: A 2018 double-blind crossover study of 121 adults reported lucid dreams on 14 percent of placebo nights versus 27 and 42 percent at two galantamine dose levels, with higher recall and vividness; its authors note it was not done in a sleep lab and relied on self-report, and Hacker News commenters raised questions about the rating scale and blinding.[27][11]

claims.claim: As a cholinesterase inhibitor it works as a memory and cognition booster in healthy people
claims.believers: Members of nootropic threads cite its acetylcholine-raising action and ask whether it would help memory retention and creativity.[17]
claims.experts: Clinical trials have enrolled people with Alzheimer disease, where reviews report modest benefit; a review of ADHD treatments reported negative findings, and no trial listed here has tested it in healthy adults for cognition.[3][6][15]

claims.claim: Multi-ingredient nootropic blends containing small amounts of galantamine improve brain function
claims.believers: Threads on commercial brain-booster products describe users combining galantamine with huperzine A, piracetam and others and reporting effects.[16]
claims.experts: No published trial has tested these blends; the evidence base for galantamine concerns single-agent use in specific conditions.[1]

claims.claim: Galantamine's dream effects will improve sleep and next-day looks and energy.
claims.believers: Users describe vivid dreams and a sense of mental clarity as part of a self-improvement routine.[13][14]
claims.experts: The 2018 trial measured dreams and mild side effects including insomnia and next-day fatigue in a minority; no study has measured sleep quality, appearance or daytime performance outcomes in healthy users.[27]

claims.claim: Lucid dreaming is harmless and has no downsides.
claims.believers: Many dreamers describe it as enjoyable; some report years of practice without issue.[29]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes long-term effects are not extensively studied and that people with some mental illnesses may find it hard to separate lucid dreams from reality; online commenters report sleep disruption.[29][11]

claims.claim: A prescription dementia drug is easy to substitute for the dream-supplement market.
claims.believers: Posters ask whether commercial blends containing small amounts work similarly.[16][17]
claims.experts: The US label describes serious skin reactions and effects on cardiac conduction as warnings for the prescription product, and Baird has cautioned against unnecessary supplements.[12][28]

card.summary: A snowdrop-derived cholinesterase inhibitor that nootropic and dream communities use for cognition and vivid or lucid dreams.
card.note: Prescription drug; nausea, GI bleeding and liver injury are among reported risks.

quick.overview:
Galantamine is a prescription alkaloid originally from snowdrop plants, approved for mild to moderate Alzheimer disease. In nootropic and dream circles it is used off-label for sharper thinking and more vivid dreams, which people fold into sleep and self-improvement routines.

A 2018 pre-sleep study on lucid dreaming is the best-known human work behind the dream claims, while most trials concern Alzheimer disease and a few other conditions.
quick.risks: Common effects are nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness and headache; serious ones include allergic reactions, serious skin reactions, stomach bleeding, liver injury and effects on heart conduction such as slow heart rate. It is Rx-only in the US and EU, and drugs that inhibit CYP2D6 or CYP3A4 can raise its levels.
quick.how: Users describe taking it in the early morning or before sleep, often with a choline source or vitamin B6, and then returning to sleep to work on dream recall and lucid dreaming. It also appears in multi-ingredient nootropic blends. Because it is a prescription drug, forum threads often tell newcomers to read up on it first.
